Lessons.Title: Notice and Wonder
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will apply your understanding of equal groups to create a Notice and Wonder activity.
This lesson provides an opportunity to observe the ways in which you notice and describe equal groups. After the warm-up, you create your own Notice and Wonder activity and then facilitate it with other you in the class. You can find images to use for your Notice and Wonder from books or other sources.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Equal Groups (10 minutes). The original locally referenced image has attribution to Virginie Duboscq via Pixabay; original pixels were not inspected. Invite multiple grounded mathematical observations and questions, without assuming a specific visible object count.

Activity 1 Design Your Notice and Wonder (20 minutes): find an image that encourages class discussion of equal groups. Write likely observations and questions; avoid giving away a predetermined answer.

Activity 2 Facilitate Your Notice and Wonder (15 minutes): display your selected image, ask the class what they notice and wonder, allow one minute of peer discussion, invite responses and record the ideas.

Independent illustration, not the source image: three equal rows containing four dots each show 12 dots. A mathematically valid notice is repeated equal groups; a useful wonder is whether another arrangement keeps 12.

Teacher assesses whether the chosen picture is appropriate, whether questions allow exploration, participation and accurate recording of classmates' original ideas. The publisher reflection Cool-down is gated and not copied.
Source-authentic activity scripts are teacher mediated. Figures, print-only masters and publisher-gated Cool-downs not independently inspected are not claimed source-identical.

KeyConcepts.Title: Preserved valid source-bound concepts
KeyConcepts.Definition:
Key ideas:
- Apply understanding of equal groups to create a Notice and Wonder activity
- This lesson provides an opportunity to observe the ways in which you notice and describe equal groups
- Compare actual values or measured attributes, not the visual size or position of a drawing.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use in conjunction with the individually verified 2021 activity directions.
KeyConcepts.Example: Learning goal: You will apply your understanding of equal groups to create a Notice and Wonder activity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Notice and Wonder
KeyConcepts.Definition: An invitation to describe mathematical observations and generate investigable questions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Invite different justified observations rather than one predetermined answer.
KeyConcepts.Example: I notice three equal rows; I wonder whether the total changes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: Groups containing an equal number of objects.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Represent group count and group size separately.

KeyConcepts.Title: Student facilitation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Lead peer discussion and record classmates' own contributions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Show the image, listen, prompt and capture answers accurately.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent equal-group demonstration
WorkedExamples.Question: With 3 separate rows of 4 dots, give a notice, wonder and total.
Steps: Notice three equal groups of four.
Wonder if the same dots can be arranged in 4 groups of 3.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 12 dots, with more than one defensible notice and wonder.
WorkedExamples.Check: Explain the mathematical relationship, and keep independently authored examples distinct from source worksheets.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating this open discussion as a single machine-marked number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source purpose is students' facilitation and mathematical conversation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for notice, wonder and discussion.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Attributing independent dots to the original publisher image.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original image pixels were not reviewed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the dot example first-party independent.
